title: Supply and Demand on a Graph
bigQuestion: Who really decides the price of a sneaker, a concert ticket or a gallon of gas?

story.title: The Sneaker Drop
story.kicker: At 10 a.m. a new sneaker goes on sale, and by noon the resale price has doubled.
paragraphs: Maya set three alarms for Saturday. A sports brand was releasing a new sneaker online at 10 a.m. sharp. The store price was $120 (an example price). Maya had saved her birthday money and her dog-walking pay for two months. At 9:58 she was on the website, finger ready over the button.

At 10:00 the page froze. At 10:01 it said SOLD OUT. The company had made only a few thousand pairs in each size. Many more people than that wanted them. Maya refreshed the page again and again. The button stayed gray.

By noon, the same sneakers showed up on a resale app. People who got a pair were selling them for $240 (an example price). That is double the store price. Maya's older brother said, "That's a rip-off." Her friend Jordan said, "No, that's just what people will pay."

Maya did not buy the resale pair. But she kept wondering. Why did the store charge $120 if people would pay $240? Why did the price jump in just two hours? And would it fall again next month? This chapter gives you the tools to answer her questions.
story.think: Who do you agree with, Maya's brother or her friend Jordan? What would make the resale price go down?

lessons.title: The Law of Demand
lessons.mainIdea: When the price of a good goes up, people buy less of it; when the price goes down, they buy more.
reading: Picture a lemonade stand at a summer park. At $3 a cup, the stand sells 100 cups on a hot day. When the owner drops the price to $2, it sells 150 cups. At $1, it sells 220 cups. These are example numbers. The pattern is what matters: a lower price, more cups.

Economists call this the *law of demand*. When the price of a good rises, the amount people want to buy falls. When the price falls, the amount people want to buy rises. The amount people are willing and able to buy at one price is the *quantity demanded*.

Why does this happen? At a higher price, some buyers decide the lemonade is not worth it. Others buy one cup instead of two. Some switch to a water fountain. At a lower price, new buyers join in. Notice the key words: willing AND able. Wanting a thing is not enough. You must also have the money to buy it.

words.d: the rule that when price goes up, the quantity people buy goes down, and when price goes down, it goes up
the amount of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at one certain price

look.title: Movie Night Snacks
look.text: A movie theater sells popcorn for $9 a bag (an example price). One week it runs a special: popcorn for $5. The manager counts the bags sold each night.
look.prompt: Predict what happens to the number of bags sold during the special. Use the law of demand to explain why.

check.q: A store raises the price of a slice of pizza from $3 to $4. What does the law of demand predict?
choices: People will buy the same number of slices
The store will run out of pizza
check.why: The law of demand says a higher price leads to a lower quantity demanded.

check.q: Which buyer is part of demand for a $60 video game?
choices: Sam, who wants it but has only $10
Lee, who has $80 but hates video games
Ana, who wants it and has $70
Rob, who wants it but is not allowed to buy games
check.why: Demand counts buyers who are both willing and able to pay. Only Ana wants the game and has enough money.

check.q: At $2 a stand sells 150 cups. At $3 it sells 100 cups. How many fewer cups sell at the higher price?
check.why: 150 minus 100 equals 50 fewer cups at the higher price.

lessons.title: Reading a Demand Schedule
lessons.mainIdea: A demand schedule is a table that shows how many units buyers want at each price.
reading: Economists often put demand in a small table. The table is called a *demand schedule*. It has two columns. One column lists prices. The other lists the quantity demanded at each price. Here is an example for a school's frozen yogurt cups: at $4, 40 cups; at $3, 70 cups; at $2, 100 cups; at $1, 140 cups.

Read it from top to bottom. As the price falls by $1 each step, the quantity rises. From $4 to $3, quantity goes up by 30 cups. From $2 to $1, it goes up by 40 cups. Every row tells the same story as the law of demand.

You can also turn the table into a graph. Put price on the side (the vertical axis). Put quantity along the bottom (the horizontal axis). Mark a dot for each row and connect the dots. The line slopes down from left to right. That line is the *demand curve*. High prices sit at the top left with small quantities. Low prices sit at the bottom right with big quantities.

words.d: a table that lists the quantity demanded at each price
a graph of the demand schedule; it slopes down from left to right

look.title: Frozen Yogurt Demand (example)
look.cite: Made-up example schedule for a school frozen yogurt sale
look.prompt: How many more cups are demanded at $1 than at $4? Does this table follow the law of demand?

check.q: In the frozen yogurt table, how many cups are demanded at $3?
check.why: Find the $3 row. It shows 70 cups.

check.q: On a graph of demand, which way does the demand curve slope?
choices: It is a straight up-and-down line
check.why: High prices go with small quantities and low prices with large ones, so the curve slopes down from left to right.

check.q: On a supply and demand graph, what goes on the vertical (side) axis?
check.why: By custom, economists put price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

lessons.title: What Shifts Demand
lessons.mainIdea: A change in income, tastes, related goods or the number of buyers moves the whole demand curve.
reading: Sometimes buyers want more at EVERY price. Say a famous athlete wears a certain backpack in a big game. Before the game, 500 backpacks sold each week at $50 (an example). After the game, 800 sell at that same $50. The price did not change. Something else did. When buyers want more at every price, the demand curve moves to the right. That is an *increase in demand*.

Four main things shift demand. Income: when families earn more, they often buy more of many goods. Tastes: a trend or ad can make a good more popular. Related goods: a *substitute* is a good used in place of another, like a scooter for a bike. If scooters get cheaper, demand for bikes falls. The number of buyers: a new neighborhood brings more customers.

A drop in demand moves the curve to the left. If a news story says a snack is unhealthy, fewer people want it at every price. Buyers' expectations matter too. If people expect a price to rise next week, they may buy more today.

words.d: buyers want more of a good at every price; the demand curve shifts to the right
a good that can be used in place of another, like tea for coffee
the money a person or family earns from work or other sources

look.title: The Rainy Summer
look.text: It rains almost every day in July. A beach town sells sunscreen at the same price as last year, $8 a bottle (an example). Stores sell far fewer bottles. Meanwhile, umbrella sales at the same stores jump.
look.prompt: Did the demand for sunscreen shift left or right? What about umbrellas? Name the cause.

check.q: A new apartment building opens next to a small grocery store. What happens to demand at the store?
choices: It shifts left because of fewer buyers
It shifts right because of more buyers
It does not change because prices stayed the same
check.why: More buyers is one of the shifters of demand. More buyers means more demand at every price, a shift right.

check.q: The price of streaming services falls sharply. Streaming is a substitute for movie tickets. What happens to demand for movie tickets?
choices: The quantity demanded of tickets rises
check.why: When a substitute gets cheaper, people switch to it, so demand for the other good falls and shifts left.

check.q: Which of these would NOT shift the demand curve for pizza?
choices: A popular show makes pizza trendy
The price of pizza itself goes up
The price of tacos, a substitute, goes up
check.why: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve. It does not shift the curve.

lessons.title: Shift or Slide?
lessons.mainIdea: A change in the good's own price slides along the curve; a change in anything else shifts the curve.
reading: This is the most common mistake in all of economics. Look closely at two events. Event one: a store cuts the price of hot chocolate from $3 to $2, and sales rise from 50 to 80 cups a day (example numbers). Event two: a cold snap hits, and at the same $3 price sales rise from 50 to 90 cups. Both show more cups sold. But they are different.

In event one, only the price changed. Buyers moved to a new point on the SAME demand curve. Economists call this a *change in quantity demanded*. It is a slide along the curve. In event two, the price stayed at $3. The cold weather made buyers want more at every price. That is a *change in demand*. The whole curve shifted right.

Here is a simple test. Ask: did the price of this good change? If yes, it is a slide along the curve. If something else changed, like weather, income or a trend, it is a shift. Never say a price change "shifts demand." A price change never moves the demand curve for that good.

words.d: a move along the demand curve caused only by a change in the good's own price
a shift of the whole demand curve caused by something other than the good's own price

look.title: Two Headlines
look.text: Headline A: "Theater cuts ticket price to $6; crowds grow." Headline B: "Hit movie wins big award; crowds grow at same $10 price." Both use example prices.
look.prompt: Which headline describes a slide along the demand curve and which describes a shift? Explain your test.

check.q: A bakery lowers the price of muffins, and it sells more muffins. What happened?
check.why: Only the muffin price changed, so buyers slid along the same curve. That is a change in quantity demanded.

check.q: A heat wave hits and people buy more fans at the same price. What happened?
choices: Quantity demanded of fans increased because of price
check.why: The price stayed the same and buyers wanted more because of weather, so the whole demand curve shifted right.

check.q: What is the simple test for a shift versus a slide?
choices: Ask if the store made a profit
Ask if the price of the good itself changed
Ask if the weather was good
check.why: If the good's own price changed, it is a slide along the curve. Any other cause is a shift.

lessons.title: The Law of Supply
lessons.mainIdea: When the price of a good goes up, sellers offer more of it; when the price goes down, they offer less.
reading: Now switch sides. Imagine you bake cookies to sell at school. If cookies sell for $0.50 each (an example), you might bake 20. It is not worth much of your time. If they sell for $2 each, you might bake 100. You would give up a movie night to bake. A higher price makes the work worth it.

This is the *law of supply*. When the price of a good rises, sellers offer more of it. When the price falls, they offer less. The amount sellers are willing and able to sell at one price is the *quantity supplied*.

Why? A higher price means more money for each unit. It can cover the extra costs of making more, like more flour, more hours and more oven time. It also pulls new sellers in. If cookies sold for $2, your friends might start baking too. A low price does the opposite. Some sellers decide it is not worth it and stop.

words.d: the rule that when price goes up, the quantity sellers offer goes up, and when price goes down, it goes down
the amount of a good sellers are willing and able to sell at one certain price

look.title: Snow Shoveling
look.text: After a big Chicago snowstorm, neighbors offer $10 to shovel a driveway (an example). Few teens show up. The next storm, neighbors offer $30 a driveway.
look.prompt: What do you predict happens to the number of teens willing to shovel? Which law explains it?

check.q: The price farmers get for corn rises. What does the law of supply predict?
check.why: The law of supply says a higher price leads sellers to offer a larger quantity.

check.q: Which way does a supply curve slope on a graph?
check.why: Higher prices go with larger quantities supplied, so the supply curve rises from left to right.

check.q: Why do new sellers enter a market when the price rises?
choices: They are required to by law
The higher price makes selling worth their costs
The price of the good is falling
check.why: A higher price means more money per unit, which can cover a new seller's costs.

lessons.title: A Supply Schedule
lessons.mainIdea: A supply schedule is a table that shows how many units sellers offer at each price.
reading: Supply fits in a table too. It is called a *supply schedule*. Here is an example for a pottery club that sells mugs at a craft fair: at $4, 20 mugs; at $6, 35 mugs; at $8, 50 mugs; at $10, 60 mugs. As the price rises, the club is willing to make more mugs.

Read the change row by row. From $4 to $6, the club offers 15 more mugs. From $8 to $10, it offers only 10 more. Making extra mugs gets harder as the club runs short of clay, kiln space and members' time. Costs rise, so each price jump brings a smaller increase.

Put the table on a graph with price on the side and quantity on the bottom. The dots rise from left to right. The line through them is the *supply curve*. It slopes the opposite way from the demand curve. That difference matters, because the two curves will cross.

words.d: a table that lists the quantity supplied at each price
a graph of the supply schedule; it slopes up from left to right

look.title: Pottery Club Mugs (example)
look.cite: Made-up example schedule for a school pottery club
look.prompt: How many more mugs does the club offer at $10 than at $4? Does the table follow the law of supply?

check.q: In the pottery table, how many mugs does the club offer at $8?
check.why: Find the $8 row. It shows 50 mugs.

check.q: Using the pottery table, what is the change in quantity supplied from $4 to $10?
check.why: 60 mugs minus 20 mugs equals 40 more mugs.

check.q: How is a supply curve different from a demand curve?
choices: The supply curve is always higher
The supply curve slopes up; the demand curve slopes down
check.why: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so supply slopes up. Buyers want less at higher prices, so demand slopes down.

lessons.title: What Shifts Supply
lessons.mainIdea: A change in costs, technology or the number of sellers moves the whole supply curve.
reading: Supply can shift too. Say a pizza shop makes 300 pizzas a week at $12 each (an example). Then the price of cheese doubles. Each pizza now costs more to make. At the same $12 price, the shop makes only 220 pizzas. When sellers offer less at every price, the supply curve moves left. That is a *decrease in supply*.

Three main things shift supply. *Input costs*: the prices of things used to make a good, like cheese, wages or rent. Higher costs shift supply left. Technology: a faster oven lets the shop make more pizzas for the same cost, so supply shifts right. The number of sellers: when new shops open, supply shifts right.

Nature and events matter too. A drought can shrink a corn crop in Illinois, shifting corn supply left. Remember the same rule as before. A change in the good's OWN price is a slide along the supply curve. Only other causes shift the whole curve.

words.d: sellers offer less of a good at every price; the supply curve shifts to the left
the prices of the things used to make a good, such as materials, wages and rent
new tools and methods that make producing goods easier or cheaper

look.title: The New Machine
look.text: A T-shirt printing shop buys a new machine. It prints a shirt in 1 minute instead of 5. The cost of ink and shirts stays the same.
look.prompt: Which way does the shop's supply curve shift? Name the shifter and explain.

check.q: The wages a bakery pays its workers go up. What happens to the bakery's supply of bread?
check.why: Wages are an input cost. Higher input costs mean sellers offer less at every price, a shift left.

check.q: Ten new food trucks start selling tacos downtown. What happens to the supply of tacos downtown?
choices: The demand for tacos shifts left
check.why: More sellers is a supply shifter. More sellers means more tacos offered at every price.

check.q: Which event is a slide along the supply curve, not a shift?
choices: The price of lumber rises, so builders offer more lumber
A new robot speeds up car making
check.why: Only the price of the good itself changed, so sellers moved along the same curve.

lessons.title: Finding Equilibrium
lessons.mainIdea: The market price settles where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
reading: Put buyers and sellers together. Here is an example market for school spirit T-shirts. At $5: buyers want 90, sellers offer 30. At $10: buyers want 60, sellers offer 60. At $15: buyers want 40, sellers offer 80. Look for the row where the two numbers match. At $10, both sides agree on 60 shirts.

That point is *equilibrium*. The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is the *equilibrium price*. Here it is $10. The amount bought and sold there, 60 shirts, is the equilibrium quantity. On a graph, it is the spot where the demand curve and the supply curve cross.

No one sets this price by a rule. Buyers and sellers find it by trading. If the price is too high, sellers are stuck with extra shirts, so they cut the price. If it is too low, shirts sell out and sellers raise the price. Prices keep adjusting until the two sides balance.

words.d: the point where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied
the price at which buyers want to buy exactly as much as sellers want to sell

look.title: Spirit Shirt Market (example)
look.cite: Made-up example market for school spirit T-shirts
look.prompt: At which price do the two sides match? What would happen at $15?

check.q: Buyers want 200 tickets at $20 and sellers offer 200 tickets at $20. What is $20?
check.why: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At $20, both are 200.

check.q: On a graph, where do you find equilibrium?
choices: Where the supply and demand curves cross
At the top of the demand curve
At the bottom of the supply curve
check.why: Equilibrium is the one point where the two curves meet.

check.q: Example market: at $3, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 50. At $4, buyers want 40 and sellers offer 65. What is the equilibrium quantity?
check.why: The two sides match at $3, where both equal 50 units.

lessons.title: Surplus and Shortage
lessons.mainIdea: A price above equilibrium makes a surplus; a price below equilibrium makes a shortage.
reading: Go back to the spirit shirts. Suppose the club charges $15. Buyers want 40, but the club has 80. That leaves 80 minus 40, or 40 extra shirts. When quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, there is a *surplus*. The fix is a sale. Lower prices draw more buyers and cut how much sellers want to offer.

Now suppose the club charges only $5. Buyers want 90, but the club offers just 30. That leaves 90 minus 30, or 60 shirts missing. When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, there is a *shortage*. Lines form and items sell out. Sellers can raise the price, and some buyers drop out.

Both gaps push the price toward equilibrium. A surplus pushes the price down. A shortage pushes the price up. This is Maya's sneaker story. The store price of $120 was below what the market would pay. The shortage sent the resale price up.

words.d: when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded, so goods are left over
when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied, so buyers cannot get enough

look.title: Leftover Pumpkins
look.text: On November 1, a farm stand still has 300 pumpkins at $8 each (an example price). Halloween is over, and few people want pumpkins now.
look.prompt: Is this a surplus or a shortage? What will the farm stand likely do to the price, and why?

check.q: Example: at $15, buyers want 40 shirts and sellers offer 80. What is the result?
check.why: Supplied is more than demanded: 80 minus 40 equals a surplus of 40.

check.q: A concert sells out in minutes and fans cannot get tickets. What does this show?
choices: A surplus, so the price was too high
A shortage, so the price was below equilibrium
check.why: More people wanted tickets than there were tickets, which is a shortage caused by a price below equilibrium.

check.q: What usually happens to the price when there is a surplus?
check.why: Sellers with leftover goods lower the price to attract buyers, which moves the market toward equilibrium.

lessons.title: Real Prices, Explained
lessons.mainIdea: To explain a price change, ask which curve shifted, which way, and what that does to the price.
reading: Now you can explain real price changes. Use three steps. First, ask: did demand or supply shift? Second, which way? Third, trace the result. When demand shifts right, price and quantity both rise. When supply shifts left, price rises and quantity falls.

Try gas prices. Gas often costs more in summer, because more families take road trips. That is an increase in demand. If a hurricane shuts down refineries on the Gulf Coast, less gas gets made. That is a decrease in supply. Either shift pushes the price up. When both happen together, prices can jump fast.

Now the video game at launch. On day one, many fans want the game. Demand is high. A year later, most fans already own it, and demand falls. The price often drops. A price change is not magic or greed alone. It is buyers and sellers reacting to a change.

words.d: a move of a whole demand or supply curve to the left or right
any place or system where buyers and sellers trade a good or service

look.title: The Sneaker, Again
look.text: Go back to Maya's sneaker. The company made a few thousand pairs. Many more people wanted them. Resale was $240 by noon. Two months later, the company releases the same shoe again and makes ten times as many pairs.
look.prompt: Which curve shifts when the company makes more pairs? Predict what happens to the resale price and explain.

check.q: A frost destroys much of Florida's orange crop. What happens to the price of orange juice?
choices: It falls, because demand shifts left
It falls, because supply shifts right
It rises, because supply shifts left
check.why: Fewer oranges means less supply at every price. A leftward supply shift raises the price.

check.q: A new study says blueberries are very healthy, and people want more of them. What happens?
check.why: Demand shifts right. Along the upward supply curve, both the price and the quantity sold rise.

check.q: What is the FIRST step in explaining a price change?
choices: Ask whether demand or supply shifted
Draw a picture of the store
check.why: Start by deciding which curve moved; then find the direction and trace the effect on price.

review.q: A cafe raises the price of a smoothie from $5 to $6 and sells fewer smoothies. What is this?
review.why: Only the smoothie price changed, so buyers slid along the demand curve. That is a change in quantity demanded.

review.q: Example market: at $2, buyers want 120 and sellers offer 60. What is the result at $2?
review.why: Demanded is more than supplied: 120 minus 60 equals a shortage of 60.

review.q: Family incomes in a town rise. What happens to the demand for restaurant meals?
review.why: Income is a demand shifter. Higher incomes usually mean more demand for goods like restaurant meals.

review.q: A factory gets a new machine that makes phone cases twice as fast. Which curve shifts, and which way?
review.why: Better technology lowers the cost of making each case, so sellers offer more at every price.

review.q: A store has 500 winter coats left in April. What should happen to the coat price?
choices: It should fall, because there is a surplus
It should rise, because there is a shortage
It should rise, because supply shifted left
review.why: Leftover goods are a surplus, and a surplus pushes the price down toward equilibrium.

review.q: Demand example: at $10, 30 sold; at $8, 45 sold. By how much did quantity demanded change?
review.why: 45 minus 30 equals 15. The lower price led to 15 more units.

review.q: Why does a supply curve slope up?
choices: Buyers want more at high prices
Higher prices cover the extra costs of making more
The government sets it that way
Sellers always sell the same amount
review.why: At a higher price, sellers earn more per unit, which pays for the higher costs of producing more.

review.q: Hot dogs and hot dog buns are used together. The price of hot dogs drops, so people buy more hot dogs. What happens to demand for buns?
review.why: Buns are used with hot dogs. When people buy more hot dogs, they want more buns at every price.
